newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin tackles Chechnya, urges calm in Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin tackles Chechnya, urges calm in Belarus.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, facing a crisis in Belarus and uncertainty over economic policy as he recovers from heart surgery, met top ministers on Tuesday to discuss another pressing issue -- breakaway Chechnya.

His press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky, speaking at a Kremlin briefing, declined to comment on a fierce attack by the communist-led opposition over Yeltsin's decision to withdraw all Russian forces from Chechnya.
But he said Yeltsin had discussed the issue with Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov when he met them at the Barvikha residence outside Moscow.
Yeltsin moved to Barvikha last week in the latest stage of recuperation after multiple bypass surgery on November 5.
His workload is increasing and the 65-year-old leader is becoming more active in handling Russia's mounting problems.

One is the furore raised by the communist-dominated opposition in the State Duma, lower house of parliament, over a deal signed on Saturday by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the head of the rebel Chechen government, Aslan Maskhadov.
The deal was signed after Yeltsin ordered withdrawal of all Russian troops from Chechnya, including both defence ministry forces and interior ministry ones.
The opposition insists that both Yeltsin's order and the Chernomyrdin-Maskhadov deal are unconstitutional and will lead to Chechnya's secession from the Russian Federation.
The Duma is due to hold an extraordinary session on Friday to discuss the issue.
The communists have threatened to try and impeach Yeltsin -- a long drawn-out procedure which has little chance of success -- or to call for a no-confidence vote in the government.
Another problem for Yeltsin is neighbouring Belarus.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had urged both sides in the Belarus crisis to show restraint, saying this was a precondition for further integration between the two Slav states.
"President Boris Yeltsin considers civic accord and prevention of violence an absolute priority," he said.
"He expects both sides to show restraint and adopt a balanced approach, believing that this is a key condition for success in Russian-Belarussian integration."

Yeltsin sent Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to negotiate a compromise between hardline Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko and his parliamentary opponents over a referendum aimed at boosting Lukashenko's powers.

But a deal signed last Friday and hailed by Yeltsin as a huge success for Russian diplomacy collapsed in less than 24 hours and Lukashenko pressed on with his referendum despite international criticism.
On Monday he claimed an overwhelming victory in the poll, which allows him to dissolve parliament and call elections if the legislature resists his actions.
Parliamentary speaker Semyon Sharetsky dismissed the vote as a "farce" and the constitutional court was due to meet to consider the possibility of impeaching Lukashenko.

Moscow favours Lukashenko's quest for closer ties with Russia but fears his autocratic style and lack of free-market economic reforms could prove a burden for the union agreed by Yeltsin and the Belarus president last April.
Another Yeltsin worry is the economy and the 1997 budget which Duma has already rejected once.

Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin, in a letter published by the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily newspaper, signalled concern about Russia's economic course and said neither the 1997 budget nor the government's medium-term growth forecasts were realistic.
Yasin said revenue forecasts should be scaled down and both social and defence spending had to be cut, even at the risk of stoking political unrest.
